t:
(a) Designation of Accrediting Entities.—

        (1) In general.—The Secretary shall enter into agreements with one or more qualified entities under which such entities will perform the duties described in subsection (b) in accordance with the Convention, this title, and the regulations prescribed under section 203, and upon entering into each such agreement shall designate the qualified entity as an accrediting entity. 
        (2) Qualified entities.—In paragraph (1), the term “qualified entity” means—

            (A) a nonprofit private entity that has expertise in developing and administering standards for entities providing child welfare services and that meets such other criteria as the Secretary may by regulation establish; or 
            (B) a public entity (other than a Federal entity), including an agency or instrumentality of State government having responsibility for licensing adoption agencies, that—

                (i) has expertise in developing and administering standards for entities providing child welfare services; 
                (ii) accredits only agencies located in the State in which the public entity is located; and 
                (iii) meets such other criteria as the Secretary may by regulation establish.    
    (b) Duties of accrediting entities.—The duties described in this subsection are the following:

        (1) Accreditation and approval.—Accreditation of agencies, and approval of persons, to provide adoption services in the United States in cases subject to the Convention. 
        (2) Oversight.—Ongoing monitoring of the compliance of accredited agencies and approved persons with applicable requirements, including review of complaints against such agencies and persons in accordance with procedures established by the accrediting entity and approved by the Secretary. 
        (3) Enforcement.—Taking of adverse actions (including requiring corrective action, imposing sanctions, and refusing to renew, suspending, or canceling accreditation or approval) for noncompliance with applicable requirements, and notifying the agency or person against whom adverse actions are taken of the deficiencies necessitating the adverse action. 
        (4) Data, records, and reports.—Collection of data, maintenance of records, and reporting to the Secretary, the United States central authority, State courts, and other entities (including on persons and agencies granted or denied approval or accreditation), to the extent and in the manner that the Secretary requires.  
    (c) Remedies for Adverse Action by Accrediting Entity.—

        (1) Correction of deficiency.—An agency or person who is the subject of an adverse action by an accrediting entity may re-apply for accreditation or approval (or petition for termination of the adverse action) on demonstrating to the satisfaction of the accrediting entity that the deficiencies necessitating the adverse action have been corrected. 
        (2) No other administrative review.—An adverse action by an accrediting entity shall not be subject to administrative review. 
        (3) Judicial review.—An agency or person who is the subject of an adverse action by an accrediting entity may petition the United States district court in the judicial district in which the agency is located or the person resides to set aside the adverse action. The court shall review the adverse action in accordance with section 706 of title 5, United States Code, and for purposes of such review the accrediting entity shall be considered an agency within the meaning of section 701 of such title.  
    (d) Fees.—The amount of fees assessed by accrediting entities for the costs of accreditation shall be subject to approval by the Secretary. Such fees may not exceed the costs of accreditation. In reviewing the level of such fees, the Secretary shall consider the relative size of, the geographic location of, and the number of Convention adoption cases managed by the agencies or persons subject to accreditation or approval by the accrediting entity.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is only a contracting or delegation arrangement with accrediting entities, plus an individual appeal, so no outside party takes part in a federal decision. But subsection (c)(3) expressly grants adoption agencies and persons a right to sue to set aside adverse accreditation actions, with the accrediting entity treated as a federal agency under the APA. The section also authorizes the Secretary to set qualifying criteria "by regulation", and rulemaking authority counts as participation under the definition.
fable.s: An agency or person who is the subject of an adverse action by an accrediting entity may petition the United States district court in the judicial district in which the agency is located or the person resides to set aside the adverse action.

qwen_block.w: The section explicitly grants an outside party (an agency or person) the right to sue (petition the court) to set aside an adverse action taken by an accrediting entity. The definition states that participation includes 'the ability to sue the government over a decision.' Although the accrediting entity is a private or state entity, the statute treats it as an agency for judicial review purposes, and the right to judicial review is a form of participation in the decision-making process as defined.
qwen_block.s: (3) Judicial review.—An agency or person who is the subject of an adverse action by an accrediting entity may petition the United States district court in the judicial district in which the agency is located or the person resides to set aside the adverse action.

opus.w: The section allows the Secretary to set criteria for qualified entities "by regulation." Rulemaking authority counts as participation under the definition and Example 6, even though it is optional ("may"). Subsection (c)(3) adds support: it lets an outside agency or person petition a federal court to set aside an adverse action. The 'No' reading, which treats this as just a licensing or accreditation scheme, misses the rulemaking authority.
opus.s: a nonprofit private entity that has expertise in developing and administering standards for entities providing child welfare services and that meets such other criteria as the Secretary may by regulation establish
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading:** One could argue the answer is "No" because most of this section just sets up accrediting entities and their duties, and applying for accreditation is like applying for a license. The judicial review provision also concerns decisions made by non-federal accrediting entities, not federal ones.

2. **Why that fails:** The section twice lets the Secretary set criteria "by regulation." Under the definition, and Example 6, authority to issue regulations counts as participation even when it is optional ("may"). Separately, subsection (c)(3) gives outside parties a right to go to court to have adverse actions set aside, and treats the accrediting entity as an agency for that review.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes a framework for the Secretary to delegate accreditation duties to outside entities (nonprofits or state agencies) via agreement. It does not require the federal government to consult or coordinate with these entities or the public before making a decision. The outside entities are performing regulatory functions under delegation, not participating in federal decision-making through consultation. The right to judicial review is against the accrediting entity, which is explicitly defined as non-Federal, so it does not constitute suing the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: (1) In general.—The Secretary shall enter into agreements with one or more qualified entities under which such entities will perform the duties described in subsection (b) in accordance with the Convention, this title, and the regulations prescribed under section 203, and upon entering into each such agreement shall designate the qualified entity as an accrediting entity.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "qualified entities" (nonprofit private entities or state agencies) are outside parties participating in the federal decision-making process because they perform accreditation duties under agreement with the Secretary. However, these entities are acting as delegated regulators or contractors performing specific administrative functions (accreditation, oversight, enforcement) rather than consulting with the government on policy or decision-making. The section describes a regulatory framework where the Secretary delegates authority, but it does not require the Secretary to consult with these entities or the public before making a decision. The "participation" definition requires the government to consult or coordinate with outsiders *before* making a decision. Here, the outsiders are making the decisions (accreditation) under delegated authority, or the government is setting the rules. There is no mechanism described for the government to seek input from these entities or the public prior to a federal decision. The judicial review provision grants a right to sue, which *is* participation, but the question asks if the section *recommends or requires* participation in the sense of consultation/coordination before a decision. Wait, the definition says: "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." Subsection (c)(3) grants the right to judicial review of adverse actions by the accrediting entity. However, the accrediting entity is considered an "agency" for the purpose of this review. Is the accrediting entity the "federal government"? The definition says "Congress, its committees and members, federal agencies, federal officials, and federal employees are all INSIDE the federal government." The accrediting entities are "nonprofit private entities" or "public entities (other than a Federal entity)". They are *outside* the federal government. But the statute says "for purposes of such review the accrediting entity shall be considered an agency within the meaning of section 701 of such title." This is a legal fiction for judicial review purposes. Does suing a non-federal accrediting entity count as "suing the government"? The definition says "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." If the entity is not the government, suing it is not suing the government. Furthermore, the primary interaction is the Secretary entering into agreements with these entities. This is a contractual/delegated relationship, not a participatory one in the sense of consultation. The section does not require the Secretary to consult with these entities or the public before making decisions. It establishes a system where outside entities perform regulatory functions. This is not "participation" as defined (consultation/coordination before a decision).

Let's re-read carefully. "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision."
Does the Secretary consult with the accrediting entities before making a decision? No.
Does the Secretary consult with the public? No.
Does the section grant the right to sue the *government*? It grants the right to sue the *accrediting entity*. The accrediting entity is explicitly defined as "nonprofit private entity" or "public entity (other than a Federal entity)". Therefore, it is outside the federal government. Suing it is not suing the federal government.
Therefore, there is no participation.
